chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about stagnant water and performing istinja from it while a carcass was in it. So he said: Perform wudu from the other side, and do not perform wudu from the side of the carcass.

key_terms.الِاسْتِنْجَاءُ: Istinja — the act of cleansing oneself after urination or defecation using water or stones. One of the prerequisites for ritual purity.
key_terms.الْجِيفَةُ: Carcass/carrion — the dead body of an animal, which is a source of ritual impurity (najasah) in Islamic law.
key_terms.الْمَاءُ السَّاكِنُ: Stagnant water — water that does not flow, as opposed to running (jari) water. In Islamic jurisprudence, stagnant water has different purity rulings than running water, being more susceptible to contamination.
key_terms.تَوَضَّأَ: Performed wudu — performed the ritual ablution (minor purification) required before prayer.

ai.seo_question: Can I use stagnant water for wudu if a dead animal is in it?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) addresses a question about the ritual purity of stagnant water contaminated by a carcass. He rules that wudu may still be performed from the side of the water opposite the carcass, but not from the side where the carcass lies. This ruling reflects the principle that contamination spreads from the point of impurity, and that one may avoid it by using uncontaminated portions of a body of water.
